I don't see that at all. There's no comparison between the US and Canada here. Beyond that, it's arguable that nVidia's lead at this stage is more through market dominance rather than a large, defensible technological edge over other companies (AMD and all the other fabless AI chip producers). Much as IBM and Microsoft maintained market dominance for decades. We might stop and reflect whether those periods actually delivered the best cost:benefit ratio to the users of those products. And then ask whether US government policy should be geared towards benefting producers (the "what's good for GM is good for America" approach) or consumers.

So no, I don't see that protecting nVidia does anything to improve US technological competitiveness (there are arguments both ways here) nor that US tech competitiveness is necessarily at risk here. Although it may well be if US export control regulations aren't enforced.

Agreed, I too never imagined a president would meddle so directly in Nvidia’s business. Then Donald Trump described bargaining with CEO Jensen Huang over how much of the company’s chip revenue the federal government should get. Trump said he started at 20 percent and Huang talked him down to 15. Hearing a president recount that conversation, I wondered what either number had to do with national security.

In April 2025, the Trump administration told Nvidia it needed a license to export its H20 chips to China, citing the risk that the chips could end up in a Chinese supercomputer. Nvidia recorded a $4.5 billion charge tied to excess inventory and purchase obligations. By August, Washington had granted licenses for shipments to some Chinese customers. Nvidia disclosed that federal officials expected a share of licensed sales revenue and that the government had published no regulation establishing that requirement.

I can see why Washington would restrict the sale of powerful chips abroad. Officials have to weigh who will use them and what they might do with them. But a percentage of sales revenue tells us nothing about the buyer or the chip’s eventual use. If officials concluded that some shipments could go ahead safely, they should have explained what made those shipments acceptable. Once the president publicly put a price on the deal, that explanation became even more important.

Imagine trying to decide how many chips to manufacture or what to promise a customer while those terms are being worked out. A published rule gives executives, customers, and investors something concrete to plan around. It also gives the public a way to judge whether similar companies are being treated consistently. Trump’s account left me wondering how much of Nvidia’s access to a major market depended on what its CEO could negotiate with the president.

Then came the Jensen "Pardon". Trump told reporters he wanted Jensen Huang to “make a big apology” and return as Nvidia’s CEO. Trump told CNBC he had spoken with Nvidia’s board and said, “I convinced them. I made the deal.”

Exciting times in the semiconductor industry, absolutely.

I think you're underestimating how much NVIDIA matters to the overall U.S. semiconductor ecosystem.

The issue isn't whether the U.S. and Canada are literally comparable today. Tim's point is that the U.S. competitive advantage in semiconductors has become increasingly concentrated in a handful of companies. Twenty years ago, the U.S. had leadership across nearly every layer of the industry: Intel in manufacturing, Qualcomm in mobile, AMD in CPUs, NVIDIA in GPUs, Broadcom in networking, and numerous EDA and equipment vendors. Today, Intel's manufacturing leadership is gone, and leading-edge production has largely shifted to TSMC and Samsung. In that context, NVIDIA is not just another successful company. It represents one of the few remaining areas where the U.S. holds an undisputed global lead.

You argue that NVIDIA's position is primarily market dominance rather than technological leadership. I disagree. Market share alone does not explain NVIDIA's valuation or profitability. CUDA, NVLink, DGX systems, networking from Mellanox, software libraries, developer ecosystems, and years of AI-specific optimization form a technological moat that competitors have struggled to replicate. AMD's hardware may be increasingly competitive, but the surrounding software and ecosystem gap remains substantial.

My point is that nVidia probably doesn't have a decisive technical lead in any of those areas and that it is the mastery/competence across all of them and building the ecosystem first that puts them out in front and makes them very hard to challenge. In that sense, the actual technical lead of ASML and TSMC seems more substantial and nVidia easier to replace than those two. Also bear in mind that the lead of US companies like nVidia is far more tied up in people and people can - and do - walk (e.g. TSMC changes CEO - business as usual, Jensen gets fired - major crisis). Not knocking nVidia here, just don't think it's quite the same.
